Milan After Dark: How Perceptions of the City Change from a Gender Perspective

Between the night bus stop and the front door there are barely three hundred metres, yet that is where the city stops being the same for everyone. I chose Milan as a use case to delve deeper into this topic.

For many women, the hardest part of a night journey is not the wait at the stop, but the last 300 metres between the bus and the front door. It is in thinking about that short walk that people decide whether to take public transport, wait for a lift or, more simply, give up going out.

Transport-equity research usually stops at the platform: it measures how far away a stop is and how often a bus comes. Perceived safety, by contrast, is studied separately, through surveys and exploratory walks. Combining these two dimensions through Milan’s open data, however, reveals an unprecedented map of the night-time city, and of who is left out of it.

Why this is a gender question

A dark, empty street is not equally dark for everyone. For many women, the walk from a night stop is not just a physical distance, but a constant exercise in self-protection.

Hypervigilance has a cost. In the literature it is called safety work (Chowdhury & Ceccato, 2026; Chaney et al., 2024): scanning the pavements, choosing routes by streetlights rather than by shortness, gripping keys between fingers, faking a phone call, quickening one’s pace. It is invisible work that, repeated for years, turns into chronic stress, anxiety and fatigue. A burden carried long before anything happens — and regardless of whether it does.

Fear narrows the city. The most common response is not confrontation but avoidance. Evening classes are avoided, late work shifts are turned down, events are left early, people choose to take a taxi or simply to stay at home. Each of these choices is a lost opportunity or an extra cost. This too is transport poverty, despite no index recording it. A neighbourhood can have a night bus and still be functionally cut off after dark.

Those who can, pay to protect themselves. Safety has a market price. In Shanghai, women pay a premium of almost 10% to rent rooms in safer, less crowded housing (Harten, 2021). In Delhi, female students go as far as choosing lower-tier universities in order to take safer routes, spending on average 290 dollars a year more than men on travel — almost double the annual tuition (Borker, 2018).

In Milan, insecurity redraws everyday habits. According to Milano Atlante di genere, by the research collective Sex & the City, women build veritable “personal geographies” that exclude entire streets, squares and time slots. In a 2021 survey of people living in the city (Il genere e l’uso della città), 60% of respondents said they had experienced sexual harassment: 84.9% of episodes took place on the street or in a park (Andreola & Muzzonigro, Urbanistica Informazioni n. 313). The authors call for gender-disaggregated data on how the city is used. A night-time index like this one could be one place to start.

Where transport poverty is concentrated

To understand how this phenomenon is distributed across Milan, the starting point is the study by Transform Transport (Transport Poverty: Accessibility to Public Transport and Social Vulnerability in Milan), which crosses two factors on a hexagonal grid:

  • Accessibility: the Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL), calculated from AMAT’s GTFS timetables.
  • Vulnerability: the average percentile rank of six ISTAT 2021 census indicators: children, elderly residents, women, non-EU citizens, unemployment and low educational attainment.

Each index is split into thirds and crossed into a 3 × 3 bivariate map. The study then averages the results by NIL (Nuclei di Identità Locale), Milan’s 88 neighbourhood units. The most transport-poor areas sit in the north-west (Quarto Oggiaro, Figino, Quinto Romano, Baggio) and the south (Barona, Corvetto, Chiaravalle).

In a later study, Into the Night (Abdelfattah et al., 2025), the same group measured how the 15-minute city changes, using about 46,000 Google Places points of interest with real opening hours on the same H3 grid. At midnight, access to food and drink, sport and mobility services falls to 14–23% of midday levels, and access to health, education and shopping to just 3–4%. Peripheral neighbourhoods such as Chiaravalle see the sharpest drops.

These studies answer a fundamental question: is the city open and reachable at night? But the second question remains uncovered, just as decisive: is the journey to get there safe, and for whom?

Step one: mapping the last mile, street by street

I first built a “nighttime last-mile walking vulnerability” model in QGIS that scores every 25 metres of street. Everything runs from scripts, in EPSG:32632, into a single GeoPackage.

The inputs (all open data):

  • Night network stops: the 416 stops served by ATM’s night lines (NM1–NM4 and N15, N24–N27), filtered from AMAT’s GTFS feed.
  • Walkable streets: 5,278 km of OpenStreetMap footways, pedestrian streets and roads, split at every node so crossings connect.
  • Lighting: OSM street lamps (buffered 15 m), plus ways and squares tagged lit=yes (buffered 10 m).
  • Points of interest (POIs) on the street: 8,446 OSM bars, restaurants, cafes, pharmacies, cinemas and corner shops (buffered 25 m).

The method:

  • Trace a 300 m walking catchment along the street network from each night stop.
  • Cut the result into 25 m segments, 85,968 of them, covering 1,413 km.
  • Test each segment’s midpoint: is it lit, and is there active frontage nearby?
  • Score it from 0 (lit, with activity) to 3 (unlit and isolated).

The result at city scale is clear-cut: along Milan’s night network, 23% of routes near stops turned out dark and isolated. Another 50% are lit but have no active street frontage at all. Only 24% combine light and social presence.

Step two: putting the two studies on the same grid

The map was striking, but a street-by-street view has limits. It shows which blocks are dark, not which communities live with that darkness. Overlaying this map on Transform Transport’s transport-poverty grid (the technical detail of the georeferencing is in the methods section at the end), a sharp rift emerges between centre and periphery, but also between different social groups.

What the overlap shows: the double disadvantage of the outskirts

In the most vulnerable third of the city, only 44% of streets are lit, against 66% in the least vulnerable third. Night life also thins out: barely 0.4 places open after midnight per 10 km of street, against 2.1 in the wealthier areas. In 90% of the most fragile hexagons there is no staffed place open late at all.

Most of this gap follows the centre-to-edge gradient that also drives PTAL. Where transit is poor, everything is dark and quiet, whoever lives there. Yet looking only at the well-served areas, the gap persists: as social vulnerability grows, lighting falls from 83% to 64% and night venues collapse from 3.1 to 0.6 per 10 km (with a rank correlation of −0.19 across the whole city and −0.25 in the best-served third).

At neighbourhood level, the contrast becomes even clearer:

Thirteen of the thirty most fragile neighbourhoods — including Quarto Oggiaro–Vialba–Musocco, Bovisasca, Figino, Quinto Romano, Quarto Cagnino, Chiaravalle and Monluè–Ponte Lambro — have no staffed place open at night. Lodi–Corvetto is an exception for night activity (12 places), but pays a structural light deficit (only 17% of streets recorded as lit). Chiaravalle is also one of the places where Into the Night finds one of the largest day-to-night drops in access to services: the same places lose both services and social presence after dark.

Checking the map against women’s voices

Open data can suggest where risk lurks, but Milan has a valuable tool to verify it on the ground. In 2024 the municipal project x STRADA + LIBERE (run with Avventura Urbana and Sex & the City) involved women and queer people in 15 neighbourhoods to map streets, stops and parks avoided out of fear. The report’s numbers explain the scale of the problem: in Milan 57% of women are afraid of walking alone at night (against 28% of men), and 20.2% give up going out in the evening altogether (against 3.8% of men).

At neighbourhood level, maps and testimonies coincide. Where the listening groups described lively streets, the data confirm light and venues; where they reported evening emptiness, the numbers record an absence of activity.

Cases like Bicocca and QT8 show why counting streetlamps is not enough: on paper they are reasonably well-lit neighbourhoods, but residents perceive them as unsafe because after dark the desert sets in. Social presence captures this unease; light alone does not.

Going down to the single street, a revealing paradox emerges. Analysing 21 streets named in the listening groups (out of 24 identified), all 7 streets judged safe turn out to be actually lit in the data (99% of their length). But of the 14 streets named as dark and unsafe, only 5 show as unlit — via Paravia and via Zamagna in San Siro, via Rosciate and via Albona in Baggio, and most of corso Lodi in Corvetto — while as many as 9 are recorded as fully lit on the maps.

Why this discrepancy? The testimonies clarify what satellites do not see: a street can have streetlamps and still be dark on the pavement. It happens when the light is aimed only at the carriageway for cars (an urban-planning legacy of the 1960s, as the QT8 report points out), or when overly dense tree canopies, blind walls, construction hoardings and parked cars create cones of shadow.

The case of viale Gran Sasso, in Porta Venezia, is emblematic: in the data all of its 1.3 km are recorded as lit. Yet women in the neighbourhood flagged the bus stop as a critical point, smothered by vegetation that blocks the view. The lamps are there, but light is missing exactly where people get off and walk.

The lighting data is therefore reliable when it flags darkness, but tends to overestimate safety when it shows light: the real gap in the neighbourhoods is in all likelihood even deeper.

Reading the maps through a gender lens

Cross-referencing these results with the City of Milan’s socio-economic data gives an even sharper picture:

  • Those with fewer resources suffer the worst darkness. According to the Comune’s Bilancio di Genere 2026, the lowest average female incomes are recorded in Quarto Oggiaro–Vialba–Musocco (€19,442) and Baggio–Olmi–Valsesia (€22,140): exactly the darkest and least-served neighbourhoods. People who live there cannot afford to pay the “safety premium” to move elsewhere or to take a taxi every evening. In addition, according to a 2023 AMAT survey of the metropolitan area, 34% of women do not have a driving licence (against 15% of men, with peaks among the over-65s), depending far more on public transport and on walking.
  • The night is not only for parties. Night transport tends to be associated with leisure. In reality, those travelling at night are nurses, cleaners, care workers, and logistics and hospitality staff: shifts covered largely by women and migrants who live precisely in the darkest peripheries. For them the night bus is not a pastime but a work necessity.
  • More complex journeys. At city scale, around 75% of care work still falls on women (Andreola & Muzzonigro). This translates into short, chained trips outside peak hours (often with prams or shopping trolleys) that depend on the quality of pavements and on neighbourhood buses more than on the big radial metro lines.
  • A gender-aware index needs the time factor. Transform’s index includes the share of the female population, which is higher in central areas. The night model suggests, however, that the risk is concentrated elsewhere: in peripheries where the walk home is dark and empty. A gender-sensitive vulnerability indicator must cross demographics with time of day and the built environment.
  • Not all “eyes on the street” reassure. Half of the night pedestrian network (50%) is lit but deserted. But even when venues are open, quality matters: bars and pubs bring light and movement, but can become places of harassment. Pharmacies on night duty, kiosks, concierge desks, hotel receptions and staffed stations offer a far more neutral and reassuring natural surveillance.
  • The stop is a place, not a point. The Into the Night study finds that at 3 a.m. over 18% of peripheral zones face waits of up to 30 minutes (against 5–15 minutes at noon). Half an hour standing under an isolated shelter weighs far more than the minutes spent on board.

The limits of the data (and why more transparency and listening are needed)

Every analysis based on open data has margins of approximation worth bearing in mind:

  1. Unmapped darkness: on OpenStreetMap, 3,520 street lamps are recorded and the lit=no tag is rarely used. The peripheries may simply be less mapped than the centre, partly amplifying the gap.
  2. Ghost venues: the 659 staffed venues identified represent a minimum threshold (a bar in the centre is mapped better than a kiosk in the periphery). Conversely, commercial data (such as Google Places, used in Into the Night) tend to overestimate “24-hour” places, including charging stations and automatic lockers that bring no human presence to the street.
  3. Centrality and light: lighting and services naturally thin out towards the city limits. Moreover, light and activity are indirect indicators that do not replace people’s direct experience, as shown by the work of the STEP UP platform by Transform Transport.

Five moves to redesign the night

Increasing night bus services is essential, but it is not enough if the surrounding environment repels the people who should use them. To make the city truly accessible after dark, targeted interventions are needed:

  1. Design the stop for waiting: well-lit shelters, clear visibility free of obstacles or hidden recesses, real-time arrival panels to reduce waiting anxiety, and clearly signposted help points.
  2. Light the pavements, not just the cars: use Milan’s LED renewal plan to redirect light beams towards pedestrian routes and faces, pruning the vegetation that obscures the lamps.
  3. Trial on-request stops: cities like Toronto, Montréal and Paris let night bus passengers get off between stops, closer to their front door. Milan could start a trial in the 30 most vulnerable neighbourhoods.
  4. Encourage neighbourhood presence: encourage the evening opening of kiosks, staffed services and community spaces near peripheral stops, moving beyond the concentration of night life in the historic centre alone.
  5. Make listening structural (and open the data): the municipal project X Strada + Libere (2024–2027) — which involved around 200 women in 15 listening groups — has already shown the effectiveness of participatory design, leading to real lighting interventions in piazzale Gabrio Rosa and in the viale Brianza underpass (x STRADA + LIBERE | LA NOTTE). This method, also inspired by Vienna’s gender mainstreaming, must be integrated permanently into transport and public-lighting planning, starting from the 13 vulnerable neighbourhoods currently without night-time presence — and accompanied by the Comune publishing the complete dataset of city lamp locations.

What planners and the city can take from this

  • Treat the walk to the stop as part of the service. Night bus planning and street lighting are run by different departments. Joint targets, such as a lit, direct path to every night stop, would make each investment count twice.
  • Start where the layers overlap. The 30 NILs Transform flagged, and especially the 13 with no night-open place, are an evidence-based shortlist for lighting audits and night-stop upgrades. The north-west (Quarto Oggiaro, Figino, Quinto Romano, Baggio) and the south-east (Corvetto, Chiaravalle, Ponte Lambro) stand out.
  • Publish street-lighting data. The Comune’s open-data portal has a dataset on the LED transition, but not lamp locations. A point layer of public lighting would replace the weakest assumption in this analysis with a real measurement.
  • Support social presence after dark. Where there are no open shops or bars, lit stops with shelters, help points, kiosks or late-opening community spaces can do part of the job. Licensing and planning policy can encourage night activity near stops in peripheral districts.
  • Pair the maps with people’s experience. Use STEP UP-style perceived-safety surveys in the flagged neighbourhoods. They would show whether the gaps the data suggests are the ones residents, and especially women, actually feel.
  • Plan by time of day. Transport-poverty indices are usually built on all-day service. A night-time version, using night lines, lighting and activity, shows a different and more unequal city.

Closing thoughts

Feeling safe in public space is not a luxury, but the prerequisite for exercising the right to the city. Fear produces concrete harm even when it does not result in a crime: it limits freedom of movement, restricts work choices and imposes an invisible tax on daily life.

In Milan, the neighbourhoods with the worst access to public transport are also the darkest and quietest after dark: a double disadvantage that hits those who already have the fewest alternatives. The tools to see this inequality already exist and are open. What is needed now is the political will to bring together the offices that plan buses and those that design the form of streets and public spaces, listening to those who cross those streets every night.

If you work on night mobility, lighting or gender and the city in Milan or elsewhere, I would love to hear how you measure the walk home.

Data and method

To guarantee the reproducibility of the analysis, the entire workflow was automated with numbered PyQGIS scripts (from downloading the boundaries to exporting the layouts), managed within a single GeoPackage in the metric reference system EPSG:32632 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N).

1. The last-mile model (Network Analysis)

  • Extracting the night network: from AMAT’s official GTFS feed I isolated the 416 stops served by ATM’s night lines (NM1–NM4 and N15, N24–N27).
  • Pedestrian graph: I downloaded from OpenStreetMap 5,278 km of pavements, pedestrian areas and walkable roads, splitting the geometries at every node to ensure correct topological connectivity at crossings.
  • Isochrones and segmentation: starting from each stop I generated 300-metre pedestrian service areas along the real graph, dividing the resulting 1,413 km into 85,968 segments of 25 metres.
  • Composite index (0–3): on the midpoint of each segment I ran a spatial proximity analysis crossing two variables:
    • Lighting: 15 m buffer from OSM point street lamps and 10 m buffer from street axes tagged lit=yes.
    • Active street frontage: 25 m buffer from 8,446 POIs (bars, restaurants, cafés, pharmacies, cinemas and corner shops).

2. Extraction and cleaning of night activity (Overpass API)

To map the real presences after midnight I wrote an Overpass query filtering the opening_hours tags (24/7 or closing after 00:00), pubs and nightclubs. I then carried out a semantic cleaning of the dataset to separate the 659 staffed venues (which generate natural surveillance) from 199 automatic infrastructures (EV charging stations, lockers, vending machines) that bring no human presence to the street.

3. Spatial standardisation and georeferencing (H3 grid)

Since the raw data from the Transform Transport study are not released in an open format, I rebuilt the spatial dataset starting from the published maps:

  • Georeferencing: I aligned Figure 4 of the study to the official municipal boundary in Web Mercator, obtaining horizontal and vertical scale consistency with a deviation below 0.06%.
  • Hexagonal grid sampling: I generated an Uber H3 grid at resolution 9 over Milan (201 m edges, ~0.1 km²). By sampling the RGB values at each cell’s centroid and matching them to the 9 classes of the bivariate legend, I reconstructed the vulnerability tertiles (555, 530 and 499 hexagons).
  • Aggregation by NIL: I transcribed the 30 critical Nuclei di Identità Locale from Figure 5 onto the official PGT 2030 boundaries, calculating for each cell and neighbourhood the percentage of lit pedestrian network and the density of night venues per 10 km of street.
